name: immer
summary: A header-only C++ library of persistent, immutable containers, including an RRB-tree `flex_vector` with O(log n) concatenation and slicing and policy-based memory management.
intro: immer brings persistent data structures to C++ with an API that feels like the standard library. `vector` is a radix tree that stores elements in contiguous chunks (32 per chunk for pointer-sized types); `flex_vector` is an RRB tree that adds O(log n) concatenation, slicing and insertion anywhere, at a constant-factor cost of 1 to 2 times on other operations once those are used. `array` is a plain copy-on-write array, `map`, `set` and `table` are hash tries, and `box` wraps a single immutable value. Every method that would change a container is `const` and returns a new one.

The library is built for systems code without a managed runtime. Memory management is a template policy: by default immer uses thread-safe reference counting and a free-list heap, and it can plug into a tracing garbage collector instead, so it can sit inside the runtime of languages like Guile or Python. Elements are stored unboxed in the tree nodes. Transients and move semantics let code apply a batch of updates in place when a container isn’t shared, then freeze the result with `persistent()`.

Juan Pedro Bolívar Puente described the design in “Persistence for the Masses: RRB-Vectors in a Systems Language” (ICFP 2017) and a CppCon 2017 talk, and built the demo text editor Ewig on it; Bolívar Puente’s Redux-like library Lager follows the same value-oriented style. The project is maintained: 0.9.0 came out in December 2025 with experimental `immer::persist` serialization, and 0.9.1 in January 2026.
strengths: Value semantics for big data: copying a container copies a pointer, and comparing old and new versions is cheap
`flex_vector` concatenates and slices in O(log n), useful for editors and for splitting and joining parallel work
Header-only with no dependencies, packaged for vcpkg and build2
Pluggable memory policies: reference counting by default, or a tracing garbage collector when embedded in another language runtime
limits: Still pre-1.0, with sparse releases: 0.8.1 in 2023, then 0.9.0 in December 2025
Reading is slower than `std::vector`: every access walks a few tree levels instead of indexing one array

Large element types make the contiguous chunks big and slow; the docs suggest wrapping them in `immer::box`. The default reference counting is thread-safe, so every copy pays for atomic operations unless you pick another policy

story: Clojure, Scala and JavaScript libraries such as Immutable.js had made persistent collections common in garbage-collected languages, especially for interactive apps built around React. Juan Pedro Bolívar Puente wanted the same for C++, where there is no garbage collector, values are often stored unboxed for cache locality, and developers sometimes need to escape immutability for a batch of updates. Bolívar Puente started immer on GitHub in August 2016.

Bolívar Puente’s ICFP 2017 paper set out the answers: an embedding RRB tree that stores unboxed elements, tree algorithms written independently of node-layout optimisations, policy-based memory management covering both reference counting and tracing garbage collection, and transients based on reference counts and C++ move semantics, including for concatenation. Bolívar Puente presented it to C++ developers at CppCon 2017 as “Postmodern Immutable Data Structures”. Releases have been infrequent: 0.5.0 in 2018, 0.6 in 2019, 0.7.0 in 2021, 0.8 in 2022 and 2023, and 0.9 in December 2025.

choices.choice: RRB trees rather than plain radix vectors
choices.why: Relaxed nodes add O(log n) concatenation and slicing while keeping lookups and updates effectively constant, as in Clojure and Scala vectors.

Without a runtime garbage collector, efficient persistence needs reference counting; but when embedded in a language that has a collector, immer should use that instead. A template policy covers both.
Most immutable collections store pointers to boxed objects; performance-critical C++ code needs values inline for cache locality.

choices.choice: Transients through reference counts and move semantics
choices.why: If a container is the only owner of its nodes, or is an r-value about to be discarded, it can be updated in place, so functional-style code gets close to mutable performance.
